doc.title: Chuck Mancuso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 10, 2013

title: Draft pressure, teaching at Baker Hall, and his brother in Vietnam
summary: A draft board clerk warned him about Canada; a friend steered him into special-education teaching at Baker Hall to avoid the draft, while his brother served in Vietnam.

blocks.x: that time, and guys like Dave Roll and Bobby Weiss and those guys, “How come you didn’t play with the ABA?” They didn’t have an ABA. And it turns out I couldn’t go to the college. I had a scholarship from all of them and I wanted to go to McGill, because I spoke a little French, because to me that was as European as you can get, you know, up there in Ottawa. And they didn’t have any of it. So I had a scholarship there and then right before I was going to start I get this letter. Now this is the summer of ’65, Time magazine did “The Summer of the Viet Nam Graduate.” So I had two courses left to finish. And I was just finishing up and I got this September 1st — so I ran down to Board 85. I was always great with ladies, you know, talking to adult ladies you know, because I was interested in what they had to say. My mother taught me to be a nice little boy. And I thought, I said to this lady, you know, “You’ve got to understand, I have a scholarship, wouldn’t it be great? I can play ball for two years, you know?” She says, “Son, don’t you understand what’s going on? All these young men are going to Canada to get away.” And I said, “I’ll sign anything. I don’t want to stay in Canada, I just want to play basketball for two years, I’ll have a master’s and I can get my writing career.” She looked me straight in the eye and she goes, “Son, September 1st, a nice toothbrush, a clean pair of shorts, you’re Board 85’s number one.” So a guy I played ball with, Joe Lotempio, he started at Baker Hall now in Buffalo, he used to tell you, “Now if you don’t behave yourself we’ll send you to Father Baker over the bridge. Because that’s where they send the bad boys. Now I had been in exceptional education. I got out once my writing got better. And I had a couple of the English profs say don’t even go to Syracuse. You just keep writing. You have a nice style. And I thought I was going to be writing. And then Joe Lotempio said — he started in June at Baker Hall — and he said, “You’re going to be a dead writer.” He just picked me up by my neck. He was a strong guy. He said, “I’m taking you into Baker Hall. I’m going to show you a room where you’re going to teach.” I said, “I got out of Ex Ed.” “You’re going back in Ex Ed.” This will get you out of the draft. Because you won’t have to fight, to go to the war. And that’s why I got back into teaching. I’d never done teaching. I had three kids in my room, and after two and a half classes they ate me up and spit me out. And I told my parents, they went crying and yelling. We had out first house on Lancaster Street, and I said, “I can’t do it.” She goes, “You were a counselor at the Butler Mitchell, those kids were tougher than those kids, you just — you’re not going to go — you’re not going to go to that Army.” And my brother had to go, my younger brother. He went right around that time and he got fucked up in Viet Nam, I’ve got to tell you. Excuse my language. You know, beautiful kid, oh yeah. He used to send me little tapes about how crazy it was. He was a photographer too. He worked on it. He said, “I’d be in the back and they’d have these cannons all over, an ear went flying by, some brains hit me in the face, and I had to take these pictures.” And

he says, “I told them, I don’t want to do it anymore.” So anyway, so I did all kinds of teaching there. And then I came for my master’s and Tallmadge asked me to do review classes in 1969 in the library. And they loved what I was doing.
